title: Final, Final, and the File We Actually Used
premise: A rough-cut folder contains three copies of one travel clip named 'final,' 'final2,' and 'final-final.' The editor opens each one to find the right moment, then leaves the names as the episode's only unresolved mystery.

title: The In-Point Moves One Frame and Nothing Else
premise: On a short ordinary road clip, the editor nudges the in-point one frame earlier, then one frame later, and watches both cuts several times. The footage gains no context, and the choice changes no visible event.

title: Detour Becomes the Door in Captions
premise: Auto-captions turn the plain spoken word 'detour' into 'the door,' and the edit shows the correction before replaying the unchanged shot. The typo gets more screen time in the review than it had in the cut.

title: Six Tracks for One Title Card
premise: The editor stacks six identical title-card layers on the timeline, drags them into alignment, and keeps only the top one. The explanation outlasts every title card in the finished travel cut.

title: A Lecture on the Playhead's Address
premise: The editor delivers a solemn voice-over explaining the playhead and time ruler while the preview stays parked on the first frame. By the time the narration finishes, the timeline has not moved and neither has the story.

title: The Export Includes the Empty Gap
premise: A routine export opens with a short black patch because the selected range reaches a blank stretch of timeline. The traveler spots it after rendering, then re-renders the same ordinary sequence and leaves the mistake as the episode's only turn.

title: We Put the Best Frame Before the Beginning
premise: A raw cut opens on several seconds of windshield pointed at a parking line. The editor moves the shot of the day's detour notice to the front, and suddenly the rest of the footage has a reason to exist.

title: The Cut Sounds Continuous Only with Room Tone
premise: Two clips from different parked stops cut together with a hard jump in cabin noise. The editor lays a strip of room tone under the cut, and the seam disappears.

title: Where a Sentence Breaks on Screen
premise: The transcript is accurate, but the captions keep splitting sentences in the worst possible place. The editor moves only the line breaks, and the same words start making sense.

title: The First Take Sounds More Like a Person
premise: The traveler records a simple update eight times, each take more polished and less like a human being. The final cut uses the first one, stammer included.
